title: Website Navigation
article_body:
Most company websites are organized around internal convenience rather than buyer behavior. Categories that make sense to the people who built the site — arranged by department, product line, or historical sequence — create friction for buyers who just want to find information relevant to their decision. Confusing navigation is invisible, but the lost leads it creates are real.

Simplifying your navigation means organizing it entirely around the buyer's journey: what do they need to find first when they arrive, what do they need next as they consider their options, and how do they take action when they're ready? Structure that question correctly, and the navigation writes itself.

## What Belongs in the Main Navigation

The main navigation should include four types of content: links to product or service pages, your Learning Center, pricing information, and a clear way to contact you or request the primary CTA. That is generally enough. Every item you add beyond that increases cognitive load and the chance that a buyer gets distracted or confused. If an element doesn't directly help a buyer make a decision, it belongs in the footer.

## Pricing Must Be Findable

Pricing is one of the most searched topics on any business website, and one of the most commonly hidden. When buyers can't easily find pricing information, many assume the company has something to hide and move on. Including pricing — or at minimum a link to a pricing or cost page — in the main navigation signals transparency and respects the buyer's time. It also supports your content strategy: cost and price pages are consistently among the highest-traffic pages on Endless Customers sites.

## The Learning Center in the Navigation

The Learning Center should be prominently placed in the main navigation and should remain accessible from every page on the site. It is not a sub-page or a buried resource. It is one of the most important destinations on the site for both buyers doing research and your sales team looking for content to share. Position it on the left side of the navigation, where users naturally begin scanning, so it's the first stop for any visitor who wants to learn more before taking action.

## Order by Journey

Arrange navigation items in the order a buyer would naturally use them. Education and content come first — the Learning Center on the left for visitors who are exploring. Products and services follow. Pricing comes further right for buyers who are evaluating and comparing. Contact and the primary call to action are always visible. This sequence mirrors how buyers actually think and move, rather than how the company is internally organized.

## Move the Rest to the Footer

The detailed 'About Us' page, the careers section, press mentions, legal pages, and other information that serves the company rather than the buyer all belong in the footer. Visitors who need those things know to look there. Keeping them out of the main navigation gives the navigation room to do its actual job: helping buyers find what they need to make a decision.
